text: {"voice_profile":"Brisk, light third-person narration that stays close to Tuppence or Tommy and slips into their idiom ('keep her end up', 'old bean', 'If that isn't a Hun, I'm a Dutchman!'). Comedy and danger sit side by side. Short dialogue exchanges carry most of the action. Wry authorial asides deflate the drama ('a reversion that aroused in Tuppence a faint misgiving'). The narration reports the characters' own reasoning step by step, such as Tuppence 'intoxicated with the success of truthfulness' or Tommy weighing the risks 'in his usual slow and steady way'. Villains speak in heightened melodramatic idiom, which is set against the young heroes' slangy understatement.","book_context":"A 1920s thriller in alternating Tuppence and Tommy strands. Its central device is the unseen 'Mr. Brown', who hides as a nondescript background figure and whose name is used openly. Small details are planted and later paid off: the clerk called Brown and the telephone message with no telephone; the name Rita, which leads to Mrs. Vandemeyer; the false Jane Finn at a Paris pensionnat; Number 14; the recess and curtain in the Soho house; the date of the 29th; the half-recognised faces of the conspirators; the girl who cannot be made to speak. Chapter II begins Tuppence's bluffing streak and her open love of money. Chapter VIII starts Tommy's captivity and lays out the conspiracy's stakes. Neither chapter may reveal who Mr. Brown is, who Number One is, or that Jane has lost her memory.","chapters":[{"id":"003","verbatim":[{"paragraph":22,"text":"little Tuppence can look after herself, thank you!","purpose":"Tuppence's signature self-assurance, which the book keeps testing."},{"paragraph":73,"text":"“Jane Finn,” she said hastily; and then paused open-mouthed at the effect of those two simple words.","purpose":"The pivotal accident that launches the plot."},{"paragraph":78,"text":"“Who’s been blabbing? Rita?”","purpose":"Plants the clue Rita, which is followed up later."},{"paragraph":80,"text":"“No,” she replied with perfect truth. “Rita knows nothing about me.”","purpose":"Shows the comic method of bluffing by literal truth."},{"paragraph":90,"text":"Her present part was of the adventuress rather than the adventurous order, but she did not deny its possibilities.","purpose":"Distinctive wordplay in the narrator's ironic voice."},{"paragraph":107,"text":"“Life,” moralized Tuppence, “is full of surprises.”","purpose":"Her flippant poise under pressure."},{"paragraph":112,"text":"“That’ll do, Brown. You can go.”","purpose":"An exact clue that must be planted without emphasis."},{"paragraph":122,"text":"“Pay the thing, will you, old bean? I’ve got nothing smaller than a five-pound note!”","purpose":"The punchline ending, which the next chapter picks up."}],"essential":["Whittington stops Tuppence in St. James's Park. He admits he overheard her at Lyons' and followed her; she dislikes him but is not afraid. He gives her the Esthonia Glassware Co. card and the 11 o'clock appointment.","Tuppence telegraphs Tommy with her retained pencil: \"Don't put in advertisement. Will explain to-morrow.\" She weighs the ninepence against five shillings.","She arrives at the dirty office, which has a middle-aged clerk in the outer room. Whittington's sleek prosperity and shifty eye confirm her mistrust.","The offer: £100 and expenses for about three months at Madame Colombier's pensionnat in Paris, as his ward, with no communication with friends and absolute secrecy. Keep his suggestion that she pass as an American because of her accent.","Tuppence says the terms are too liberal. Whittington replies that he is paying for intelligence and discretion. She insists that her partner Beresford is included: 'both or neither'.","Asked her name, she blurts 'Jane Finn' to protect the archdeacon. She has no idea of its meaning, and the narration must state that ignorance. Keep Whittington's rage and dismay.","Keep the bluffing exchange: his question about Rita; 'How much do you know?' answered with 'Very little indeed', which worries him more; 'It might be my own name' or chance; and 'how much do you want?'","Keep her money-talk: a little down now, 'payment of services in advance' rather than blackmail, and 'I'm so very fond of money!' Keep his unwilling admiration: he took her for a meek kid with just enough brains.","The clerk brings a 'telephone message'; Whittington dismisses him by the name Brown. Do not comment on the telephone or on Brown.","He abruptly gives her fifty pounds and tells her to come back tomorrow. His 'Au revoir' turns genial again, which gives her a faint misgiving.","She leaves elated, takes a taxi to Tommy, and closes with the five-pound-note line."],"optional":["The bun purchase and her musings in the cubicle (para 26–27) can be condensed. A crashing blow descended on his head, and all was darkness.","purpose":"Cliffhanger ending."}],"essential":["Tommy climbs the filthy stairs. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password, and that entering the meeting room would be a colossal risk because more identification may be required.","He hides in the recess behind the torn velvet curtain, opposite the meeting-room door and overlooking the stairs, and watches through its slits.","Arrivals use the signal knock and are asked their number. Keep the bearded, precise-voiced German chairman's 'Your number, comrade?' and the brutal reply 'Fourteen, gov'nor' / 'Correct'. Tommy is glad he did not enter.","The other arrivals: an Irish Sinn Feiner; a quiet, shabby, clerk-like man; a working man with a vaguely familiar face; and a commanding, well-dressed man whose face Tommy half-knows but cannot name. Include Tommy's wonder at who holds this varied chain.","The pale Slavonic last arrival seems to see through the curtain. All rise for him. Mr. Brown 'cannot be present'; the guest suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye each other in fear. He is seated at the head as 'Number One', and Number Fourteen shuts the door.","Tommy removes his shoes and tries the handle with great care; the door is bolted inside. He restores the handle and his tenacity persists.","He enters the empty next-door bedroom, draws the rusty bolt on the communicating door, and hears the meeting but cannot see past the portière. He identifies speakers by voice only.","Irish business: money for a 'reign of terror' in Ireland; money routed via Irish Americans and 'Mr. Potter', with the American voice's caveat; the difficulty of landing ammunition; and the commanding man's 'Think of the feelings of Belfast'. Mention the newspaper loan and the denial from Moscow briefly.","The German reports 'by--Mr. Brown' on the unions. The date is the 29th. The Labour leaders must think the strike is their own show. Keep Number One on honest men.","'Clymes must go', assigned to Number Fourteen. Keep the gloves with a housebreaker's fingerprints and Fourteen's relish for blood running in the streets.","The German doubts the Labour leaders will strike. The document would assure success, but they do not have it. Only 'a girl' may know where it is; 'This case is different'.
